children: Electric, autonomously driven big rigs are one solution to the shipping industry's current diesel problem. That's an opportunity for Tesla.

The Iran war has pushed prices at the pump up, with diesel users hit particularly hard. A gallon of diesel fuel is around $6, nearly double the year-ago level. Crude oil prices aren't up that much, but the fighting has taken so-called heavier crude off the market, which yields more diesel fuel per barrel, all else being equal.
There's less diesel to go around at a time when freight demand is finally improving after a brutal post-Covid stretch for the sector.

Investors aren't happy with the situation. Coming into Friday's trading, the State Street SPDR S&P Transportation ETF was down about 7% over the past month. Shares of trucking companies XPO, Old Dominion Freight Line, and FedEx Freight were all down more than 10%.
Amid that backdrop, "enter Tesla Semi," wrote Morgan Stanley analyst Andrew Percoco in a Friday report, looking at how the vehicle can change the profit picture for shippers.
Tesla introduced its Semi truck in 2017 and hopes to make 50,000 a year. That's a significant number. The total volume of semi trucks sold in the U.S. and Europe each year is closer to 500,000.

A Tesla electric semi can cost twice as much as a traditional truck, but rising diesel prices help recoup the extra upfront cost quicker. What's more, some places, such as California, offer significant incentives for electric trucks, which can drive down acquisition costs.
At roughly $300,000 each, 50,000 units might generate annual sales of about $15 billion. Tesla is expected to generate 2026 revenue of $106 billion, according to FactSet.

Selling trucks, like selling EVs, isn't the biggest potential benefit to Tesla, however. Self-driving trucks remove the driver, lowering costs even further for shippers, while improving truck utilization. (Tesla's self-driving technology doesn't have to sleep.)

"Tesla can generate about $12,000 to $18,000 per month from its autonomous trucking software ($0.85 to $1 per mile subscription fee times 18,000 miles driven per month)," says Percoco. "This compares to about $100 per month for FSD on consumer vehicles today."

FSD stands for Full Self Driving, which is Tesla's highest-level driver assistance product capable of doing most of the driving most of the time. FSD is also the basis for Tesla's autonomous robo-taxi fleet.
The Semi truck opportunity could be worth up to $20 per share, according to Percoco. That's about $80 billion in market value, and the value is based on some 80,000 Tesla semis on the road by 2040.
Tesla stock was up 0.3% in premarket trading at $364.80, while S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were both up about 0.6%.

Coming into Friday trading, Tesla stock was down about 10% since the start of the Iran war, underperforming the S&P 500 by about 20 percentage points, despite higher fuel costs that make EVs relatively more attractive.
Investors just aren't focused on the cars right now. They are focused on AI-related opportunities such as self-driving cars-just like Morgan Stanley.
